content: 1. Symphysiotomy should be considered as an emergency obstetric intervention to prevent the development of obstetric fistula in cases where other options are not viable. 2. Comprehensive perioperative training programs for fistula surgeons and midwives should be developed and evaluated to enhance surgical outcomes in fistula repair. 3. The impact of physical exercise, both preand post-surgery or rehabilitation, on improving surgical outcomes should be systematically assessed. 4. Simple suturing techniques, such as 2–3 basic sutures to approximate fistula edges, may promote spontaneous closure of the fistula or improve the success rate of subsequent repair surgeries. 5. The optimal timing between the occurrence of a fistula and its surgical repair should be determined to maximize treatment success. 6. Postoperative bladder dysfunctions following fistula repair surgery should be described in detail, and the most effective interventions to prevent or treat these complications should be identified. 7. The effectiveness of one-layer versus two-layer bladder closure techniques during fistula repair surgery should be evaluated. 8. The WHO recommends specific durations for bladder catheterization following surgical repair of simple obstetric urinary fistulas, and the effectiveness of these durations should be assessed. 9. Conservative management using a Foley bladder catheter for fresh urinary fistulas should be evaluated for its effectiveness in promoting healing. 10. The role of physiotherapy in enhancing bladder function after fistula repair surgery should be systematically assessed. 11. The incidence of fistula repair breakdown or recurrence months or years after the initial repair should be studied to identify risk factors and improve long-term outcomes. 12. Rehabilitation programs for women following fistula repair should be developed and evaluated to ensure successful social reintegration. 13. Determinants of successful rehabilitation should be identified, with a focus on legal rights support, mental health needs, pediatric rehabilitation for live-born infants, and addressing patient-identified gaps in services related to maternal and infant morbidities caused by prolonged obstructed labor. 14. The dissemination and implementation of guidelines for obstetric fistula care should involve all stakeholders at international, national, and local levels to improve surgical outcomes and the quality of care for affected women. 15. Access to high-quality fistula repair and postoperative care services should be expanded and strengthened in healthcare facilities globally. 16. The WHO's GREAT Network employs an evidence-based knowledge translation approach to support lowand middle-income countries in adapting and implementing reproductive, maternal, perinatal, and newborn health guidelines. 17. The implementation of these recommendations should be monitored at health-service, regional, and country levels using indicators such as fistula repair breakdown rates, urinary incontinence rates, hospital stay duration, and maternal satisfaction with care. 18. The guideline will be updated every five years unless significant new evidence necessitates earlier revision. The WHO Steering Group will monitor research developments and address any concerns about the validity of the recommendations. 19. Suggestions for additional questions or topics for inclusion in future guideline updates are welcomed by the WHO. 20. The anticipated impact of these recommendations on the organization of care and resources is minimal, as they primarily involve optimizing existing practices in fistula care settings.
